title: The Edge of the Map: How Free Land Shaped American Democracy

intro.summary: Turner asks what made the United States different from Europe. In thirteen essays written between 1893 and 1918, he argues that the main cause was a moving 'frontier': the edge of cheap, unclaimed farmland that kept shifting west for three centuries. He says this free land made settlers more equal, more individualistic and more democratic. It also gave the poor an escape from the crowded East. When the 1890 census reported that no frontier line remained, he warned that these two pioneer ideals, freedom to get ahead and equality, would start to clash, and that Americans would turn to government regulation to protect democracy. His main limits: the evidence is mostly travellers' accounts, speeches and census maps, used to illustrate a sweeping interpretation rather than to test it. His 'free land' was in fact Native land, and phrases like 'savagery and civilization' treat Native nations as obstacles rather than peoples. This lesson does not cover his writing on sections (regions) in depth, or the long debate among later historians over the 'safety valve' and the frontier thesis. Both are good topics to study next.
background: A census counts a country's people. The United States has run one every ten years since 1790, and its maps showed where people lived.
In Turner's time, much of the western land belonged to the federal government, which sold it cheaply or gave it away to settlers. The Homestead Act of 1862 is one example.
Turner read this paper in 1893, when most historians explained American institutions by tracing them back to Europe, especially England and Germany.
The land Turner calls 'free' or 'vacant' was home to Native American nations. It was taken through wars and treaties, a fact his essays mention but do not dwell on.
intro.aha: Turner argued that American democracy grew less from the Constitution than from cheap land at the edge of the map, so when that land ran out in 1890, the pioneer's love of getting ahead began to undercut the pioneer's love of equality.
assumes: Colonial history of the United States
Native Americans in the United States
Territorial evolution of the United States

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Why is American society the way it is? In 1893 most scholars answered by pointing to European roots: laws, churches and habits carried over the Atlantic. Turner, a young historian from Wisconsin, thought this looked in the wrong direction. He proposed that the key lay in the West, at the moving edge of settlement.
primer.quote: The existence of an area of free land, its continuous recession, and the advance of American settlement westward, explain American development.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Turner started from an official report. The 1890 census said settlement was now so scattered that no frontier line could be drawn. The census defined the frontier as the edge of areas with at least two people per square mile. Turner traced how that line had crept west, from the Atlantic coast across the Appalachian Mountains, the Mississippi and the Great Plains. He gathered travellers' diaries, petitions, speeches, laws and census maps to show what happened to people and institutions along the way. His essays interpret this evidence; they are not experiments or statistical tests.
primer.quote: In the census reports it is treated as the margin of that settlement which has a density of two or more to the square mile.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: Turner argued that each new frontier stripped settlers back to simple conditions, and that society then grew up again from scratch. Because land was cheap, people there were roughly equal, suspicious of rulers and eager to govern themselves. New western states let all adult white men vote. Their pull on population forced older states to widen voting too. So, he claimed, democracy in America grew mainly from this experience of the land, not from a written plan.
primer.quote: American democracy was born of no theorist's dream; it was not carried in the Susan Constant to Virginia, nor in the Mayflower to Plymouth. It came out of the American forest, and it gained new strength each time it touched a new frontier.
primer.quote_where: Chapter XI, The West and American Ideals

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body: If free land had held democracy up, its end was a warning. Turner saw farmers and workers who could no longer move west. He also saw a few giant companies take control of iron, coal and railroads. Pioneers had prized the freedom to get ahead, but that same freedom now seemed to threaten equality, and people began asking government to step in.
primer.quote: In brief, the defenses of the pioneer democrat began to shift, from free land to legislation, from the ideal of individualism to the ideal of social control through regulation by law.
primer.quote_where: Chapter X, Pioneer Ideals and the State University

primer.heading: Limits to keep in mind
primer.body: Turner offers one big explanation built from selected examples, and he says himself that his first essay aims only to 'suggest some of the problems' rather than settle them. His evidence shows that the frontier and democracy went together. It cannot prove the frontier caused democracy, since other forces, such as the ideas of the Revolution, were at work at the same time; Turner admits this. His picture of 'free land' leaves Native peoples largely in the background, as obstacles. Later historians have challenged many of his claims, especially the idea that the West worked as an escape valve for eastern workers.

concepts.title: The frontier: a moving edge of settlement
concepts.idea: The frontier is the line where settlement thins out to about two people per square mile, and that line keeps moving west as settlement grows.

predict.question: Turner calls the frontier 'an elastic' term. Suppose the census had drawn its line where settlement falls to 6 people per square mile instead of 2, on the very same map. Where would the line fall?
options: Farther east, closer to the coast
Farther west, deeper into the interior
There would be no line at all
why: Right. Going west, the number of people per square mile keeps falling. It drops to 6 before it drops to 2, so a higher cutoff is crossed sooner, nearer the coast.
A bigger number can feel like 'more frontier', but the count falls as you go west. The curve reaches 6 before it reaches 2, so the line moves east, not west.
This fits if you picture the frontier as a real fence on the ground. It is a chosen cutoff on a falling count, so changing the cutoff moves the line.
Lines vanish when dense pockets far out west make the cutoff get crossed many times, as in 1890. A single smooth, falling curve still crosses 6 exactly once.

terms.means: How many people live on each square mile of land, like counting the people on one city block.
The official count of everyone in the United States, taken every ten years.
The place on the census map where settlement thins out to about 2 people per square mile: the outer edge of settled land.

model.title: How settlement thins out going west
model.note: Teaching model: the land is squeezed into a single west-running strip. Settlement falls off smoothly from the coast, and the far-west pockets (mining camps, ranch towns) always sit 300 and 600 miles beyond the main edge. Only the cutoff of 2 people per square mile comes from the census, as Turner reports it. The curve's shape, the miles and the pocket sizes are illustrative, not historical data.

controls.label: How far settlement has pushed west

outputs.label: Near pocket counts as settled (1 = yes)
Far pocket counts as settled (1 = yes)
Times the curve crosses the cutoff

x.label: Distance west of the Atlantic coast (hundreds of miles)

steps.say: This curve counts how many people live on each square mile as you travel west from the Atlantic coast.
The flat line marks 2 people per square mile. Land emptier than that counts as barely settled.
This slider sets how far settlement has pushed west. Watch the curve stretch out.
The marker sits where the curve sinks below the flat line. This box gives its distance from the coast.
This slider grows small settlements far out west, like mining camps. Watch the bumps appear past the edge.

explore.prompt: Move settlement west and grow the far-west pockets. Find out when the edge is easy to draw and when it falls apart.

goals.text: Move the frontier line to between 1,800 and 2,000 miles west of the coast, with the curve crossing the cutoff only once.
hints: Which slider stretches the whole curve toward the west?
The edge sits where the curve falls to 2 per square mile. Watch the edge box as you stretch, and keep the far-west pockets small.
You need the stretch slider well past the middle of its range, but not at the top.

goals.text: Break up the frontier line: make the curve cross the cutoff five times while the main edge stays east of 1,200 miles.
hints: Five crossings means two extra pockets, each rising above and then falling below the flat line.
A pocket only counts if its peak clears the 2-per-square-mile line. The far pocket sits on thinner ground, so it is the harder one to lift.
Watch the far pocket's peak. It clears the line a little past a quarter of the way along the pocket slider.

feedback.correct: Yes. The frontier line is wherever a falling count crosses a chosen cutoff. Raise the cutoff to 6 and the curve hits it sooner, nearer the coast. That is why Turner calls the term elastic.
feedback.incorrect: You may have pictured the frontier as a fixed fence. It is a counting rule: the place where people per square mile drop below a cutoff. People thin out going west, so a higher cutoff is reached sooner and the line moves east.

steps.say: Start early, when settlement hugs the coast. People crowd near the sea and thin out fast inland. The number of people on each square mile is called population density.

The census, the official count taken every ten years, marked the place where density falls to 2 per square mile. That place is the frontier line, the outer edge of settled land. Here it is only a couple of hundred miles inland.
As more families move west, the curve stretches and the crossing slides west with it. The frontier line is not a wall. It moves.
Push settlement further and the edge passes 1,300 miles. Turner followed this march census by census: from the fall line near the coast, over the Appalachians, to the Mississippi and beyond.
Now add a few thin settlements far out west. Their bumps stay under the flat line, so they don't count as settled. There is still one clear edge.
Make those pockets denser: mining camps and ranch towns that leap ahead of the main edge. Now both bumps rise above the cutoff, and the curve crosses it five times.

So which crossing is the frontier line? There is no single answer. This is the 1890 moment. The census said the unsettled land was so broken up by scattered settlement that it could no longer draw a frontier line.

understand.explanation: The census measured how many people lived on each square mile and treated land with fewer than 2 as beyond settlement. The frontier line is simply where that count drops below 2, so it is a counting rule, not a fence. As settlers poured west, the place where the count fell to 2 kept sliding west. Turner traced it decade by decade, from the Atlantic fall line to the Appalachians, the Mississippi and the Rockies. When dense pockets sprang up far ahead of the main edge, the cutoff was crossed in many places. In 1890 the census said there was hardly a frontier line left to draw. Two caveats: Turner himself calls the term 'elastic', and land counted as 'unsettled' was not empty, because Native nations lived there; the line measures only settlers counted by the census.
understand.quote: The most significant thing about the American frontier is, that it lies at the hither edge of free land. In the census reports it is treated as the margin of that settlement which has a density of two or more to the square mile.
understand.quote_where: Chapter I, The Significance of the Frontier in American History

equation.text: × ln(20 ÷ 2)   (where 20·e^{−x/s} falls to the census cutoff of 2 people per sq mi)

connect.caption: Turner's essay has no equation. This is the model's own rule. The '2' is the census cutoff Turner reports. The orange 'edge' is the frontier line, found where the main curve 20·e^{−x/s} drops to 2. The blue 's' is how far settlement has pushed west: double it and the edge moves twice as far from the coast. The starting crowd of 20 per square mile is illustrative.

concepts.recap: The frontier line is just where settlers per square mile drop below 2. It marched west with settlement until scattered pockets broke it up in 1890.

concepts.title: Starting over: each frontier rebuilds society
concepts.idea: At every new frontier, settlers fall back to simple conditions and society develops again in steps (trader, rancher, pioneer farmer, town), so the process keeps repeating as it moves west.

terms.means: The order in which ways of making a living arrive in a new region: fur trader first, then cattle-raiser, then pioneer farmer, then settled farms, towns and factories
Turner's picture of these stages passing one spot in single file, like a parade, one after another
A page that was written on, scraped, and written over, so the old writing still shows faintly. Turner uses it for a region whose earlier stages still leave traces under the newer ones

concepts.recap: The frontier did not just move west. At each new edge, society dropped back to simple conditions and rebuilt itself in roughly the same order of stages, though never identically.

understand.explanation: You already know the frontier was a moving line. Turner's next claim is about what happened at that line: settlers lost most of the comforts of the place they left and had to start again with simple tools, a log cabin and a small clearing. The region then developed again in steps, which this lesson calls frontier stages: fur trader, cattle-raiser, pioneer farmer, then settled farms, towns and finally factories. Turner pictured this as a procession of civilization: stand at Cumberland Gap and you would see 'the buffalo following the trail to the salt springs, the Indian, the fur-trader and hunter, the cattle-raiser, the pioneer farmer' go by, and a century later the same parade passed South Pass in the Rockies. Because each stage is laid over the one before, Turner calls an older region a palimpsest, a page written over many times where faint traces of the earlier writing still show. This is Turner's interpretation, built from travelers' accounts, emigrant guides and census maps rather than measured as a law. His wording ('savagery', 'primitive') reflects his era, and his own text admits settlers followed Native trails and clearings, so the land was not empty; he also says the stages overlapped and differed by place and time.
understand.quote: Thus American development has exhibited not merely advance along a single line, but a return to primitive conditions on a continually advancing frontier line, and a new development for that area. American social development has been continually beginning over again on the frontier.
understand.quote_where: Chapter I, 'The Significance of the Frontier in American History'

activities.title: One region, many layers: Wisconsin, as Turner describes it

steps.text: Fur trade. In the early 1800s Wisconsin's main outposts were the fur-trading posts of Green Bay, Prairie du Chien and Milwaukee. French and Canadian boatmen paddled birch canoes along its rivers to trade with Native nations. Britain stayed the dominant power there until after the War of 1812.
Mining and first pioneers. Next, the lead mines in the southwest corner drew settlers from Illinois and the South.

Farm rush. After the Black Hawk War of 1832, soldiers reported how rich the soil was. Settlers from western New York and New England poured in through Milwaukee, and German immigrants followed. Turner gives the population as 30,000 in 1840 and 300,000 in 1850.
Single crop. For a time the state was 'given over to almost exclusive grain-raising'. Turner compares it to North Dakota in his own day, which was going through that same stage further west.
steps.result: Stage: wheat farming on new soil

steps.text: Varied farming. As the soil wore out under the same crop every year, farmers turned to varied crops and dairying. Some organized creameries.
Factories. In Turner's words: "Thus Wisconsin, now developing manufacture, is a State with varied agricultural interests."

This is the palimpsest at work. What is now a manufacturing state was earlier a farming area, and before that a trading ground. Each later layer covers the earlier ones without erasing them completely.

activities.takeaway: The same order of stages ran in one place over about a century. When it finished in Wisconsin, it was already starting again in North Dakota. That repetition is what Turner means by 'beginning over again'.

activities.title: Frontier or settled?
activities.prompt: These descriptions come from the stages Turner and the emigrant guide he quotes (Peck, 1837) describe. Sort each one: does it belong to the early frontier stage, or to the later, rebuilt society?

cards.text: A log cabin, about a dozen cleared acres, a corn crop and a small 'truck patch' garden
cards.feedback: Frontier. This is Peck's first wave, the pioneer who lives on what he can grow, hunt and graze, with homemade tools.

cards.text: A family lives partly by hunting and by letting stock graze the open 'range'
cards.feedback: Frontier. Living off wild game and unfenced grass is a sign that settlement has only just arrived.

cards.text: A trader exchanges guns and goods with Native nations for furs
cards.feedback: Frontier. The fur trader was usually the very first stage. Turner says traders moved far ahead of farmers.

cards.text: Drovers herd cattle from scattered cow pens to markets hundreds of miles away
cards.feedback: Frontier. Turner notes that cattle could 'transport itself' to market, which suited remote places with no roads. This is the rancher's frontier.

cards.text: Hewn log houses with glass windows and brick chimneys, plus mills, schoolhouses and courthouses
cards.feedback: Later. This is Peck's second wave, people who buy the land and 'exhibit the picture and forms of plain, frugal, civilized life'. Society is being rebuilt.

cards.text: Brick buildings, colleges and churches, with silks and fashions in the shops
cards.feedback: Later. This is Peck's third wave, the 'men of capital and enterprise', when the village becomes a town or city.

cards.text: Farmers switch from growing only wheat to dairy and varied crops
cards.feedback: Later. Turner describes this shift in Ohio and Wisconsin once the cheap new soil was used up and land grew dear.

cards.text: Factories open and the main town grows into a manufacturing city
cards.feedback: Later. Manufacturing is the last stage on Turner's 'continental page', the end point that Wisconsin was reaching in his day.

activities.takeaway: The early stages lean on what the land offers for free: game, grass, furs, new soil. The later stages add buildings, institutions and industry. Turner's point is that every newly settled region passed through this sequence again.

activities.question: A made-up case: in 1840 a farmer sells his land in a well-built Ohio town and moves to unsettled land in western Iowa. According to Turner's idea, what are his first years likely to look like?

options.text: He brings Ohio's mills, schools and brick houses with him, so his new place is settled from day one
options.feedback: Turner argues the opposite. At the frontier 'the environment is at first too strong for the man'. Settlers lose most of what the older society had built and must start with simple conditions.

options.text: He drops back to simple conditions (cabin, small clearing, a few animals), and the region then rebuilds through the stages
options.feedback: Correct. This is the 'return to primitive conditions' followed by 'a new development for that area'. Ohio's stages repeat in Iowa.

options.text: Nothing develops: Iowa stays a wilderness because the frontier has moved past it
options.feedback: The frontier moving on does not leave a region empty. Turner says each frontier 'leaves its traces behind it' as the area fills in and becomes settled.

options.text: Iowa jumps straight to factories, because the country as a whole was already industrializing
options.feedback: Turner does not describe stages being skipped like this. New regions started with farming and grew industry later. (He does say later frontiers moved faster, as the next question shows.)

activities.question: Turner says the process repeats at each frontier. Does he claim every frontier looked exactly the same?

options.text: Yes. The same stages, at the same speed, everywhere
options.feedback: Not what he says. He warns of 'essential differences due to the place element and the time element'.

options.text: No. The order is similar, but place and time made real differences: a mining frontier differs from a farming one, and a railroad-era frontier moved faster than one reached by canoe
options.feedback: Correct. Turner contrasts the farming Mississippi Valley with the mining Rocky Mountains. He also notes that in early New England the stages 'succeeded rapidly and intermingled'. The pattern is a tendency, not a fixed recipe.

options.text: No. He says there is no pattern at all, and each region was completely unique
options.feedback: That overcorrects. He insists there are similarities: the solutions worked out on one frontier 'served as a guide for the next'.

concepts.title: Free land as an escape hatch
concepts.idea: Because a worker could leave for cheap western land, eastern employers had to pay at least what moving west was worth, so free land pushed up wages even for people who never moved.

predict.question: Imagine a new canal makes the trip west cheap. But the government now sells western land only in huge lots that cost far more than any worker could save. What happens to eastern factory wages?
options: They barely change, because workers still cannot actually take a western farm
They rise a lot, because moving got much cheaper
They fall, because the canal brings more workers into the East
why: Correct: the escape hatch only pushes wages up if a worker can really use it. With the land out of reach, it works like the switch turned off, however cheap the trip.
Cheaper travel helps only when there is affordable land at the end of the trip. Here a worker gains nothing by going, so employers feel no pressure.

The canal could carry people either way, but this idea is about workers' option to leave. With no reachable land, that option is gone, so wages rest at what employers would pay anyway. The option does not push them down.

terms.means: The best deal a worker could get by walking away, such as running a western farm instead of taking a factory job
The lowest pay an employer can offer and still keep workers. Here the outside option sets it
Turner's picture of free western land as a way for pressure in the East, like low pay and crowding, to escape

model.title: What an eastern worker earns at home versus out West
model.note: Teaching model: one kind of worker, one eastern wage and one value for a western farm. The cost of moving is spread into a monthly amount, and the land switch is all or nothing. Employers simply match the better of their own wage and the western deal. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. Turner gives no wage figures, and later historians dispute how strong this effect really was.

controls.label: Monthly value of a western farm
Monthly cost of getting there and starting out

outputs.label: What going west is worth after costs
Extra pay caused by the open West

steps.say: Picture a worker in an eastern mill town in the 1800s. These bars compare his pay at home with what he could get out West.
This grey bar is what employers would pay if nobody could ever leave.
This slider sets how much a western farm is worth to a family each month.
This one is the cost of the trip, the tools and the hard first years, spread month by month.
And this switch says whether cheap western land is still there to take.

explore.prompt: You are the West. Change what a farm is worth and what it costs to get there, and see how hard you can squeeze eastern employers.

goals.text: Make the open West add at least $15 a month to the eastern wage.
hints: The wage moves only once the 'going west' bar rises above the grey bar.
The western deal is the farm's value minus the moving cost. It has to beat the $30 home pay by the extra you want.
Leave the moving cost alone, and the farm must be worth a little more than at the best point in the walkthrough.

goals.text: Keep the farm's value where it starts, but still get the open West to push the eastern wage above the pay employers would offer if nobody could leave.
hints: If the farm can't get better, what else decides whether going west is a good deal?
Lower the cost of getting there, and watch the 'going west' bar.
The 'going west' bar has to climb past the grey bar, and that takes a very cheap move.

feedback.correct: Right. The escape hatch raises wages only if workers can really take it. A cheap trip to land nobody can afford gives no better deal, so employers feel no pressure.
feedback.incorrect: You may have thought a cheaper trip is enough by itself. The wage floor is the farm's value minus the cost of getting it. If the land is out of reach, the western deal is worth nothing, and wages stay at what employers would pay anyway.

steps.say: Start here. A western farm is worth $40 a month, but moving eats $30 of that. Going west nets only $10, far below the $30 job. Nobody is tempted, and the wage stays at $30.
Now better land opens up, worth $60 a month. After moving costs, going west nets $30, exactly what the job pays. Workers are right on the edge of leaving.
Make the farm worth $70. Going west now nets $40. An employer who still offers $30 will watch his workers pack up.
So he raises pay to $40 to keep them. The eastern wage climbs even though, in this picture, nobody has actually left. The deal a worker could get by walking away is called his outside option.

That outside option sets a wage floor: the lowest pay an employer can offer and still keep workers. Turner called the West in this role a safety valve, where pressure in the East could escape to free land.
Now close the land, as the 1890 census said the frontier had closed. The outside option disappears, and the wage drops back to $30.
Reopen the land but make the move expensive. Even with good land, going west nets only $20, so the wage stays at $30. The option protects workers only if they can afford to use it.

understand.explanation: An employer has to pay only a little more than a worker's next-best choice. While cheap western land existed, that choice could be a farm of one's own. So eastern pay could not sink far below what a farm was worth after the cost of getting there, and that pushed wages up even for workers who never left. Turner did not measure wages. He argued this from the record: New England factory owners opposed cheap-land laws, and a congressman in 1796 warned that closing off western land would force some class to work 'for such wages as they please to give.' Later historians doubt the effect was strong, because the trip and a new farm cost more than most factory workers could save. Some argue that farmers' sons going west instead of into factories still eased the pressure.
understand.quote: it underlay much of the later opposition of New England as a manufacturing section to the free homestead or cheap land policy, demanded by the West and by the labor party, in the national public domain. The migration of labor to free lands meant that higher wages must be paid to those who remained.
understand.quote_where: Chapter II, The First Official Frontier of the Massachusetts Bay

check.task: Keep the move costly, at $25 a month or more, and still force the eastern wage up to at least $50 a month.
check.hint: What counts is the farm's value minus the moving cost. If the cost stays high, the farm must be worth a lot more.
check.misconception: That a costly move always kills the escape hatch. In fact the pressure depends on the gap between the farm's value and the cost of reaching it, not on either one alone.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not an equation from the paper: Turner argues in words and gives no formula. The eastern wage w_{East} is the larger of two amounts. One is the pay employers would offer if no one could leave (w_{0}). The other is the western deal: the farm's value V minus the cost of moving C, which counts only while land is open (L = 1).

concepts.recap: The chance to leave for cheap land set a lowest wage that eastern employers had to beat, even for workers who stayed. Historians still debate how strong that pull really was.

concepts.title: Frontier pressure widens democracy
concepts.idea: Coastal elites kept power by giving each county equal seats, even where interior counties held more people, but the growing West pushed states to count people instead and to let more men vote.

predict.question: South Carolina's up-country had become the larger part of the population but had too few seats. In 1808 the coast's 'lower section' kept control of the senate, and the up-country got the house. A new law needs both houses. What did this deal give each side?
options: Each side could block the other, but neither could pass laws alone
The up-country could now pass any law it wanted
The coast kept full control, as before
Seats in both houses now matched population exactly
why: Correct. Each section held one house, and a law needs both. Turner calls this 'a mutual veto', a halfway step between rule by counties and rule by head count.
You might think so because the up-country won the larger house. But the coast still held the senate, so it could stop any law the up-country passed.
You might think so because the coast kept the senate. But once it lost the house, the coast could no longer pass laws alone, so it no longer had full control.
You might expect reform to mean counting people everywhere. Here each house was handed to a section instead, so neither house's seats were simply matched to population.

terms.means: The rule for dividing a legislature's seats among places, such as one or two seats for every county
Giving each area seats in proportion to how many people live there, so every person's say weighs the same
The right to vote. 'Widening suffrage' means letting more people vote, for example men without property

model.title: Who holds the seats: the coast or the inland?
model.note: Teaching model: a state has two regions only, the coast and the inland beyond the river falls. The coast is fixed at 19,000 men and a slider sets the inland's men. Under the county rule every county gets the same number of seats. The model shows only how seats are divided, not who may vote. The figures of 19,000 men and 'more than 30,000' are Jefferson's, quoted by Turner. The county counts (30 on the coast) are made up for illustration and are not historical data.

outputs.label: One coast man's say ÷ one inland man's say

steps.say: Picture a state like colonial Virginia. The blue bars are the coast: its share of the state's men, and its share of seats in the law-making assembly.
The orange bars show the same two shares for the inland, the newer country upriver beyond the falls, where boats can no longer pass.
This slider sets how many thousand men live inland. The coast always has 19 thousand.
This slider sets how many counties the inland is split into. The coast has 30 small ones.
This switch picks how seats are handed out: so many per county, or according to the number of men.
And this number shows how many times one coast man's say outweighs one inland man's.

explore.prompt: You run the state's constitutional convention. Try to shift power using only what each rule actually counts.

goals.text: Keep seats handed out by county, but give the inland a majority of the seats.
hints: Under the county rule, do more inland men change the seats at all?
Seats follow the number of counties. Which slider adds counties to the inland?
The coast has 30 counties in this model, so the inland needs more than that.

goals.text: Switch to counting men, yet leave the coast holding most of the seats.
hints: Once men are counted, the seats simply follow the 'share of men' bars.
For the coast to win, which side has to have more men?
The inland must have fewer men than the coast's 19 thousand.

feedback.correct: Right. Each section held one house, and a law needs both, so the deal created a mutual veto. The up-country could stop the coast and the coast could stop the up-country. It was a compromise between counting counties and counting people.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what each side controls. The coast kept the senate and the up-country got the house, and a law needs both. So neither side could pass laws alone, but each could block the other. Turner calls this 'a mutual veto'.

steps.say: Start with equal numbers: 19 thousand men on the coast and 19 thousand inland. Seats go by county, and the coast has 30 counties to the inland's 10, so the coast holds 75% of the seats.
Now use Jefferson's own numbers: more than 30 thousand men inland. The inland now has about 61% of the men, yet its seats have not moved at all.
This is Jefferson's complaint: 'the 19,000 men below the falls give law to more than 30,000.' One coast man's say now weighs almost five times an inland man's.

Let the West keep growing. The inland is still stuck at 25% of the seats. Under this rule, growth alone never wins power. Only new inland counties could do that, and coastal assemblies created very few.
The rule for dividing seats is called apportionment. Giving every county equal seats let a shrinking minority keep the majority of seats.
Now flip the switch to count men instead. This is representation by population. The seats jump to match the men, and the larger inland takes control.

Back at Jefferson's numbers, now with men counted: the inland holds about 61% of the seats and the weight is 1, so every man counts the same. Western pressure also widened suffrage, the right to vote, which this model does not show.

understand.explanation: Many early states gave every county the same number of seats. The old coast had many small counties and the interior had a few huge ones. So, as you just saw, the interior could fill up with settlers and still hold only a minority of the seats: Jefferson complained that 19,000 men below the falls made the laws for more than 30,000. Turner gathers cases colony by colony, such as Pennsylvania, where three old counties and Philadelphia elected 26 delegates while the five frontier counties elected 10. He argues that the growing West, together with older states' fear of losing their people to freer new states, pushed conventions to count people more fairly and to let more men vote. This is an interpretive argument built from selected examples, not a measured effect. Turner also credits the ideas of the Revolution and the rising power of city workers as further pushes toward democracy.
understand.quote: Not only did they add new recruits, but by their competitive pressure for population they forced the older States to break down their historic restraints upon the right of voting, unless they were to lose their people to the freer life of the West.
understand.quote_where: Chapter V, The Ohio Valley in American History

connect.caption: Turner gives no equation, so this is the model's own rule. Under the county rule, the coast's share depends only on the number of counties (green), so inland growth (orange) changes nothing. When men are counted (the switch), the share depends only on population. The 19 is Jefferson's 19,000 coastal men; the 30 coastal counties are illustrative.

concepts.recap: Equal seats per county let a coastal minority rule a growing West, until frontier pressure forced states to count people and widen the vote.

concepts.title: When the land runs out, two ideals collide
concepts.idea: Free land let individualism and equality grow together. Once it was gone, unchecked competition concentrated wealth and threatened equality, so pioneers' heirs turned to government regulation to protect democracy.

predict.question: A new online farming game opens with a huge empty map where anyone can claim free plots. Two years later the map is full and a few players own most of it. Players who loved the free-for-all now ask the makers to cap plots per player. By Turner's idea, why?
options: With no empty plots left to move to, open competition piles land into a few hands, so players turn to rules to keep chances fair.
Players have lost interest in getting ahead and now just want everyone to own exactly the same amount.
The game makers' rules caused the plots to pile up in a few hands in the first place.
Nothing really changed: players always wanted caps and simply had no way to ask before.
why: This is Turner's mechanism. While the map had room, a crowded player could always start fresh, so competing and staying equal went together. Once the map filled, the same competition concentrated plots, and rules became the stand-in for open land.

Tempting, because asking for caps sounds like giving up on ambition. In Turner's account the pioneers' heirs kept their drive to get ahead. They gave up some free competition only to protect equal chances, and they did not ask for equal shares.
Some people blame whatever rules exist. In the model, and in Turner's argument, the piling up comes from unchecked competition once open land is gone. Rules arrive afterwards as a response.
Tempting if you assume people's wishes stay fixed. Turner's point is that conditions changed: open land made caps unnecessary, and its disappearance created the demand for them.

terms.means: The belief that each person should be free to push for their own success with little interference, like a player who wants no limits on how much they can build.
Turner's picture of free land as a way out: when the crowded East pressed on someone, they could leave for cheap western land, much as a valve lets off pressure.
Wealth and control gathering into a few giant companies or fortunes, such as a handful of railroad and steel firms.
Government rules that limit what businesses may do, for example caps on railroad rates or laws breaking up giant firms.

model.title: What happens to the pioneers' ideals as free land runs out
model.note: Teaching model: Turner's argument is turned into a five-part cause-and-effect sketch with made-up weights. Turner gives no numbers or formula. 'Equal footing' stands in for democracy in his sense of equal chances. 'Drive to get ahead' stands in for the pioneer's competitive spirit. Real history had many other causes the sketch leaves out, such as immigration, railroads and gold. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Does more drive help (+) or hurt (−) equal footing?

steps.say: This is a map of causes and effects in the pioneer West. Each circle is a force. Each arrow shows one force pushing another: thick when strong, and marked as helping or hurting.
This slider sets how much cheap land is still open in the West.
This one sets how hard people push to get ahead. Watch the arrows out of that circle thicken.
This one adds government rules that limit big business.
These boxes give the results: room to get ahead, big fortunes, equal footing, and whether more drive helps or hurts equal footing.

explore.prompt: Play with the moment the frontier closes. Find where getting ahead stops helping equality, then look for a way to protect equality once the land is gone.

goals.text: Keep some free land open, yet make more drive to get ahead hurt equal footing instead of helping it.
hints: Watch the help-or-harm box while you move just one slider.
It's the free land slider: with all the land open, more drive helps, and with none it hurts. The flip lies somewhere in between.
The sign turns negative a little past the middle of the land slider. Settle just below that point, not at zero.

goals.text: The frontier is fully closed. Lift equal footing above 30% while leaving people more than 25% room to get ahead.
hints: Free land can't come back, so something else has to do the job it used to do.
Turn up the government rules slider and watch the big fortunes circle shrink.
Rules at half strength aren't enough. Push them well past halfway, and keep the drive in the middle of its range rather than at the top.

feedback.correct: Right. Once there is nowhere new to go, open competition concentrates what's left, and people who still value fairness reach for rules as the substitute for open land. That is Turner's story of the Grangers and Populists.
feedback.incorrect: The likely assumption is that people's values changed. In Turner's account the values stayed the same and the conditions changed: open land had let getting ahead and equality grow together, and its disappearance set them against each other, which is why rules were demanded.

steps.say: Start in the open West: all the free land is still there. Big fortunes sit at 0% and equal footing is high, at 88%.

Turn drive all the way up: equal footing hits 100%. Turner calls this push for your own success individualism. With empty land everywhere any striver can claim a farm, so land is a safety valve: a way out of the crowded East.
Now fill in some of the land, leaving 70% open. A new arrow appears from drive into big fortunes, at 30%. Equal footing slips to 67%. The help-or-harm box is still positive, but only barely.

1890: the census finds no frontier line. With no land left, the same drive flows into big fortunes, now 100%. This is concentration of capital: wealth gathering in a few giant firms like railroads and steel trusts.

Look at the help-or-harm box. It went from +30 to −50. The drive to get ahead is unchanged, but its effect on equal footing has reversed, and equal footing has fallen to 0%. That reversal is the collision between the two ideals.

The pioneers' heirs, the Grangers and Populists, answered by asking government to set rules on railroads and trusts. This is regulation. Rules curb the fortunes and soften the harm, but they also shrink room to get ahead, from 100% to 75%.

Turner's big claim: American democracy grew less from the Constitution than from cheap land at the map's edge. When that land ran out in 1890, the pioneer's love of getting ahead began to undercut the pioneer's love of equality.

understand.explanation: While free land lasted, individualism and equality pulled in the same direction: anyone who strove could claim a farm, and that way out kept the East's employers and bankers from locking people in place. Turner argued that once the 1890 census found no frontier line, the same competitive drive began piling wealth into a few hands. He pointed to the steel trust and Harriman's railroad combinations. That concentration threatened the equal chances democracy rested on. The pioneers' descendants then turned to government, through Granger, Populist and Progressive demands for railroad rules, income taxes and controls on trusts. Turner warned that these rules protect equality but also endanger creative individualism, and that both ideals had to be kept. This is an interpretive argument built from selected historical examples, not a measured test of cause and effect. Later historians have questioned how many eastern workers actually used the West as a way out.
understand.quote: But American democracy was based on an abundance of free lands; these were the very conditions that shaped its growth and its fundamental traits. Thus time has revealed that these two ideals of pioneer democracy had elements of mutual hostility and contained the seeds of its dissolution.
understand.quote_where: Chapter XII, 'Social Forces in American History' (1910)

check.task: Put the model in a state where the frontier is fully closed and there are no government rules, yet big fortunes stay below 15%.
check.hint: Big fortunes need two things at once. Free land is gone and rules are off, so which force is left that you can still turn?
check.misconception: That the closing of the frontier by itself created big fortunes. In Turner's account it is the unchecked drive to get ahead, meeting a closed frontier, that piles up wealth. The collision needs both.

connect.caption: This is the model's own rule, not Turner's: he wrote essays, not equations. L is the free land left and R is the strength of government rules. The first term is the help that drive gives equal footing while land is open. The second is the harm that drive does through big fortunes once land is gone, reduced by rules. The sign flips when land runs low.

concepts.recap: Free land let getting ahead and staying equal grow together. When it ran out, the pioneer's competitive drive turned against equality, and rules had to take land's place.
